title: Envy (Avot 4:21)
hook: envy, desire and honor-seeking drive a person from the world

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: ka'as, anger. Your line was anger is idolatry. Did a breath get between the heat and your hands? Today, a quieter trait that burns slower. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-seven.

A thumb scrolls. Someone's new kitchen, all white marble. Someone's promotion, with a long string of congratulations underneath. Someone's beach. Nothing bad has happened. The day was fine a minute ago. And yet something has shifted in the chest, a small sour pull, and the fine day looks a little smaller than it did. Pirkei Avot has a short line about that pull, and it doesn't treat it as small. It names it alongside two companions and says what the three of them do to a person. Today's word is the first of them.
screen: `A THUMB SCROLLS.` → `NOTHING BAD HAPPENED.` → `THE DAY LOOKS SMALLER.`

segments.voice: Kin'ah. Envy. Turn it four ways. First, the saying. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar teaches in Pirkei Avot: envy, desire, and the chase after honor drive a person out of the world. Out of the world. Readers take that in more than one way. Some hear it about this life: an envious person can stand in a beautiful place and not be there at all, because their attention is always next door. Others hear it about the world to come. Both readings agree that envy takes something away from the one who feels it. Second, the body. Proverbs puts it physically, in the King James words: "A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones." The proverb doesn't place the damage in the person envied. They're on the beach. It places it in the one holding it, from the inside, slowly. Third, a surprise. The Talmud has a kind word for one kind of kin'ah. In tractate Bava Batra it says that the envy of scholars increases wisdom. Seeing a classmate learn more can push you to study harder. So the same Hebrew word can name a rot or a spur. The difference seems to lie in direction: envy that wants the other person to have less, or envy that makes you reach for more yourself. Fourth, the way back. Ten days ago this path heard Ben Zoma's answer about honor. His question just before it, in the same chapter of Avot, fits here: who is rich? He answers: the one who is happy with their portion. Not the one with the most. The one who can look at what's on their own table and actually see it. That's the opposite of being driven out of the world. It's being let back in.
screen: `ENVY, DESIRE, HONOR: OUT OF THE WORLD.` · `THE ROTTENNESS OF THE BONES.` · `THE ENVY OF SCHOLARS.` · `HAPPY WITH THEIR PORTION.` · then, large: `ENVY REMOVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one envy. Settle, and breathe. Name one person you've envied lately. Say it plainly to yourself; nobody else is listening. Now ask which kind it is. Does it want them to have less? Or does it point at something you'd like to grow toward? If it's the second kind, keep the direction and drop the sourness. If it's the first, picture setting it down like a bag you've carried too long. Then look at your own portion. Name three things on your own table, real and ordinary. Stay with them until they look as solid as the thing you were envying. If you pray, you can give thanks for your portion in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Kin'ah. Envy. Avot names it among the things that drive a person out of the world, though the Talmud allows that the envy of scholars can increase wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: envy removes. Today, when envy stirs, ask whether it wants them to have less or you to grow, and then look at your own table. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Jews study Pirkei Avot, including Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's teaching on envy and Ben Zoma's 'who is rich'; Mussar students often take envy as a trait to work on, alongside gratitude for one's portion.

fork.setup: your study partner is learning faster than you, and you feel the sting. which kind of kin'ah does the Talmud praise?
options: letting it push you to study harder.
fork.reveal: Bava Batra says the envy of scholars increases wisdom: envy that makes you reach for more, not wish the other less.

original.note: Hebrew: envy or jealousy; the same word can also mean zeal.

trapdoor: what you thought: envy is a passing sour mood.
what it means: Avot says envy, with desire and honor-seeking, drives a person out of the world.
what a scholar hears: kin'ah can also be a spur; the Talmud says the envy of scholars increases wisdom, so the trait is judged by its direction.

sources.quoted: A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.

notes: Avot 4:21 (numbering varies, 4:21 or 4:28): Rabbi Elazar HaKappar on envy, desire and honor. The two readings of 'out of the world' (this life / the world to come) are given as 'some... others'; confirm.

Proverbs 14:30 quoted from KJV because the JPS 1917 wording ('A tranquil heart is the life of the flesh; but envy is the rottenness of the bones') was not certain. A Keeper may prefer JPS 1917 for this path.
Bava Batra 21a: 'kin'at sofrim tarbeh chochmah' (the envy of scribes/scholars increases wisdom); paraphrased. Confirm.
Original note: kin'ah can also mean zeal (as with Pinchas); confirm phrasing.
Ben Zoma (Avot 4:1) may have appeared earlier in the year; used briefly as the antidote. The practice's 'three things' is the listener's own list, not a factual count.

Editor: Ben Zoma's riddle was the hook of day 1267, so 'who is rich' is now framed as an explicit callback rather than a fresh discovery; 'envy doesn't harm the person envied' narrowed to what Proverbs 14:30 actually pictures.
